passage:
I'm Keerthana, the neighbour on the second floor. Last Saturday I was watering my balcony plants when a cricket ball crashed through the landing window below. Chaitanya, a boy of about ten, stood frozen with the bat. His father came out shouting, "What will the neighbours say? Get inside, don't tell anyone!" Chaitanya's face went grey. He scooped the ball, and glass stayed on the stairs.
All Sunday morning I saw him take the long way round, past the back gate. I don't know for sure what he was thinking. But that afternoon he knocked on my door and asked in a small voice if I would come with him to tell the watchman about the glass, before a small child stepped on it.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya's father shout after the window broke?
qa.a: He shouted, 'What will the neighbours say? Get inside, don't tell anyone!'

qa.q: What might Chaitanya have been feeling when his face went grey?
qa.a: He was probably afraid and embarrassed about being seen, though the narrator says the exact thoughts are not certain.

qa.q: What turning point shows Chaitanya thinking beyond fear of gossip?
qa.a: He knocked on Keerthana's door and asked Keerthana to come and tell the watchman about the glass so a small child would not step on it.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya's father have seen the broken window?
qa.a: He seems to worry more about what the neighbours will say than about the glass or the ball, so his first move was to hide it.

grounding: A child warned about what the neighbours will say fears public embarrassment before considering right and wrong.

subtopic: Honour and shame vs guilt cultures
passage:
Monday: Elizabeth, eight, tore a page of a library book by accident. Mummy saw it and said quickly, "What will the librarian think? What will people say about us? Hide it in your bag." Elizabeth's stomach turned over.
Thursday: She took the long way to class so she wouldn't pass the library. When her friend Bhavna asked why, Elizabeth whispered, "Everyone will talk."
Tuesday: Bhavna said, "I tore a page once. Miss just gave me tape and said thank you for telling." She walked beside Elizabeth to the desk. Elizabeth put the book down with both hands and said, "This got torn, and I'm sorry."
The librarian reached for the tape.

qa.q: What did Mummy say to Elizabeth after the page was torn?
qa.a: She said, 'What will the librarian think? What will people say about us? Hide it in your bag.'

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling as she took the long way to class?
qa.a: She was afraid and ashamed of being talked about, fearing that everyone would know about the torn page.

qa.q: What made the difference on Tuesday when Elizabeth returned the book?
qa.a: Bhavna told a torn-page story of Bhavna's own and walked with Elizabeth to the desk, so Elizabeth could say sorry and hand the book back.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have seen Elizabeth's fear?
qa.a: Bhavna seems to understand it, having torn a page once too, and stayed beside Elizabeth to show that telling the librarian could be safe.

grounding: A child told what people will say learns to fear embarrassment before understanding right and wrong, until a friend eases it.

subtopic: Honour and shame vs guilt cultures
passage:
In Accra, Kofi, nine, knocked over a tin of blue paint on the church steps while decorating for Easter. His grandmother, Auntie Vera, gasped. "Kofi! What will people say? The whole church will talk about our family!"
Kofi's stomach twisted. He didn't think about the steps. He thought about the faces of the ladies in the choir.
The next week, he broke a cup at home and hid the pieces under the sink.
When his father found them, he sat Kofi down. "Why did you hide it?"
"So nobody would talk about us."
His father sighed. "Kofi, the cup matters because it was Grandma's, not because of neighbours. When you make a mistake, you own it and fix it. Not because of what people say. Because it's right."
Kofi went to Auntie Vera and told her about the cup himself.

qa.q: What did Kofi knock over on the church steps?
qa.a: He knocked over a tin of blue paint.

qa.q: What was Kofi thinking about when his stomach twisted?
qa.a: Kofi felt ashamed and afraid, thinking about the faces of the choir ladies rather than the steps.

qa.q: What did Kofi's father teach him that fear of gossip didn't?
qa.a: He taught Kofi to own and fix mistakes because it is right, not because of what people might say.

qa.q: How might Auntie Vera feel when Kofi tells her about the cup himself?
qa.a: She might feel surprised and touched by his honesty, and perhaps rethink how she reacted about the paint.

grounding: Outside India, a child warned about what people will say learns to hide mistakes out of fear, until a parent teaches him to own them.

subtopic: Honour and shame vs guilt cultures
passage:
At the school's annual day, Kalyani, ten, forgot her lines in the middle of the play. She stood frozen on stage for five long seconds until the teacher whispered from the wings.
Backstage, her mother, Minakshi, grabbed her arm. "In front of the whole colony! What will people say about us now? Sharma Aunty was sitting in the front row!"
Kalyani's face burned. She didn't cry until they got home. That night she asked, "Can I leave drama?"
The next morning, her class teacher took her aside. "You froze, then you finished. That's brave. Everyone forgets lines sometimes."
"But Amma says people will talk."
"Some will, for a day. What matters is that you practised and kept going."
Kalyani nodded, but she still flinched when she saw Sharma Aunty at the gate.

qa.q: How long did Kalyani stand frozen on stage?
qa.a: She stood frozen on stage for five long seconds.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani ask if she could leave drama?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and afraid of what people would say after her mother's reaction, more than about the mistake itself.

qa.q: How did the class teacher help Kalyani?
qa.a: The teacher praised her for finishing, said everyone forgets lines, and focused on effort rather than on what people might say.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have reacted differently to help Kalyani?
qa.a: Minakshi could have comforted her first and praised her for finishing, instead of worrying about Sharma Aunty and the colony.

grounding: A child who forgets her lines is told the neighbours will talk, and learns to fear embarrassment more than to understand the mistake.

subtopic: Honour and shame vs guilt cultures
passage:
Monday. Sumit, eight, kicked his ball into Verma Uncle's balcony and broke a flowerpot. His mother, Usha, hissed, "Don't tell anyone! What will the building say? That we can't control our son?"
Wednesday. Verma Uncle asked the children who broke his pot. Sumit said, "Not me." His ears went hot. He couldn't sleep that night.
Saturday. Sumit told his father everything. His father didn't shout. "Sumit, the question isn't what the building will say. It's what's fair to Verma Uncle. He loved that plant."
Sumit's mother was quiet, then sighed. "I taught you to hide it. That was wrong of me."
That afternoon, Sumit and his mother went to Verma Uncle with a new pot and a small tulsi plant. Sumit said sorry. Verma Uncle smiled. "Thank you for telling me."

qa.q: What did Sumit and his mother take to Verma Uncle?
qa.a: They took a new pot and a small tulsi plant.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when his ears went hot?
qa.a: Sumit felt guilty and anxious about lying, which is why he couldn't sleep.

qa.q: What turned the situation around?
qa.a: His father reframed it as what was fair to Verma Uncle, not what the building would say, and his mother admitted she was wrong to teach hiding.

qa.q: How might Verma Uncle feel when Sumit says sorry?
qa.a: Verma Uncle would likely feel pleased and touched by Sumit's honesty, thanking him for telling.

grounding: Over several days, a child told to hide a mistake for fear of gossip lies and feels guilty, until his parents teach him to own it because it is right.

subtopic: Honour and shame vs guilt cultures
passage: Jasleen, you're scared the neighbours heard you shouting at your brother? Let me tell you something. When I was nine, I broke the Sharmas' flowerpot with my cricket ball. My mother didn't ask if I had said sorry. She grabbed my arm and whispered, "What will people say? The whole gali will talk." So I learnt to hide things. The next time I broke something, a cycle bell, I buried it behind the water tank. I wasn't sorry; I was scared of being seen. Years later my teacher, Master Iqbal, caught me copying. He didn't mention anyone else's opinion. He just asked, "Is it right?" That question stayed with me longer than all the gossip. So ask yourself that one, Jasleen. Your Chaitanya Dadu is still learning it.

qa.q: What did young Chaitanya bury behind the water tank?
qa.a: He buried a cycle bell he had broken.

qa.q: What did young Chaitanya feel when he buried the cycle bell?
qa.a: He felt scared of being seen rather than sorry, which shows shame had taught him fear, not conscience.

qa.q: At the turning point, why did Master Iqbal's question work better than "What will people say?"
qa.a: "Is it right?" made Chaitanya judge his own action instead of worrying about gossip, which built a conscience that lasted.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya's mother have reacted with "What will people say?"
qa.a: She was probably embarrassed and worried about the family's name in the gali, so her first fear was the neighbours' talk, not the lesson.

grounding: It illustrates a child warned that a mistake will make the neighbours talk, who learns to fear being seen before understanding right and wrong.
